points.why: It credits the hours saved, people skipping optional meetings, and better capture of action items.
It traces summaries becoming the unchecked record, fewer voices and less dissent, and absent readers acting on flattened nuance, all with clear mechanisms.

Third-order effects are labeled speculative and include skill erosion and junior staff losing exposure, but only one effect is tied to a known pattern (the reinforcing loop) rather than each checked against archetypes.
Remedies include a named person confirming action items, decision meetings with expected attendance, and random spot checks against recordings, all of which keep the gain.

pitfalls.why: It recommends a pilot and safeguards rather than rejecting the tool.

notes: Describing the EU and UK as 'all-party consent' regimes oversimplifies how recording rules work there, and legal exposure is filed under second-order effects even though the answer calls it immediate.
